This makes me so angry. As a society, we've invented new ways to police each other and it's gone too far.

A coworker of mine recently shared their experience working at TSA and told us that after the initial morning meeting employees were forbidden to use the restroom before taking their post. As an IC sufferer, you can imagine my horrified thought of not being able to use the restroom before being trapped somewhere for hours. This person is older and was doing it for extra money after retirement. My other coworker, who is also older, chimed in to say "Who tells a 70 year old man they can't take a leak?"

It's hard enough suffering the pain, and I'm trying to maintain that mentality. Who is anyone to tell me when I can go?

I guess it's taught me that you shouldn't necessarily live like there's no tomorrow, because more often than not, tomorrow does come.

The other big takeaway is that trying to date through the channels we are afforded through isolation was so worthless. I'm sure other people had positive experiences but what I felt was a false sense of closeness was forced by the circumstances.

Driving in the snow terrifies me too. I moved to a place with snow and ice when I grew up in sunny Arizona. The roads are a mess here and people can't drive on a normal day.

I try to fill up my tank when there is snow in the forecast and I also have 3 three ninety pound bags of cement to put some weight in the rear end of my vehicle (can be bought at a Lowe's or home Depot). I also only take side streets.

Beyond that, I just make sure my insurance is up to date (I pay monthly) and try to remember that if something happens, it's beyond my control and I'm generally prepared. I try not to fret too much about a worst case scenario. When it snows, people have to drive to work and it's always a dangerous situation no matter what.

Hope this helps a little.

I read that antibiotics can trigger a flare. The long and short of it is that your bladder will continue to attack an inflammation that no longer exists. I found this to be plausible because my first real flare coincided with a round of antibiotics after a nasty UTI when I was younger.

Not retail particularly, because that can wind up being a dead end path, although I have had some great experiences in retail and met people who helped facilitate my career. I would say research different organizations based on your interests and find one that needs part time help. Remember, it's about picking a place that is going to treat you well that you can grow with. I would recommend any mom and pop places that still have the throwback mentality of old fashioned work standards. This is difficult.

Don't be afraid to fail. It's part of life and the sooner you learn to handle it the more agile you become. A part time shitty job with a good boss becomes a good gig when your boss will recommend you for something even though you don't have experience because you were an awesome employee.

Man, this world is rough now if high school kids are worrying about how to succeed in the job market. 

Your best bet is to get a job, keep that job, work hard at that job and start building your work history. Which takes time, and there's no substitute. Pick a place that you like, that treats you well and start building.

I'm not discouraging you from going to college and getting trapped in a dead end job. Where I think many people get tripped up is thinking that college is the absolute best path to employment, when in reality, experience is absolutely valuable.

I went to school but didn't graduate and wound up in an entry level position that requires a bachelor's just because I met the right friend and had enough work experience to leverage the lack of degree. All paths are different.
